# AI's land problem is pushing data centers into the ocean (Fortune / The Conversation)

By Nir Kshetri (Professor of Management, University of North Carolina – Greensboro) and The Conversation. Published August 25, 2026, 9:34 AM ET. Republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license (original: https://theconversation.com/ai-companies-look-to-the-ocean-as-a-place-to-put-more-data-centers-289180).

## Key findings
- The AI boom's demand for data centers (energy, water, carbon) is pushing developers to explore the ocean as a location for AI infrastructure, in hopes that underwater data centers improve energy use and cooling efficiency while using less fresh water and land.
- Microsoft launched Project Natick in 2015; the 2018 Orkney Islands (Scotland) seafloor unit (864 servers) failed at about one-eighth the rate of comparable land-based servers. Microsoft ended the project in 2024 and chose not to build more underwater data centers (possible reasons: regulatory/environmental permits, faster upgrades).
- China built what may be the world's first wind-powered underwater data center in Shanghai (Lingang); launched June 2025, full commercial operations May 2026. US$226 million project; uses seawater as coolant; uses at least 30% less electricity than traditional data centers; offshore wind turbines cut fossil-fuel reliance and carbon emissions.
- Japan: floating-platform container data center near Yokohama (opened 2025), solar-powered, test continues through March 2027. Singapore: Keppel's four-story floating data center (2026 build, opens 2028), seawater cooling. South Korea (Ulsan, 2025): planning an underwater data center for 100,000+ servers, ~30% less power via seawater cooling. Maine (US): DeepGreen Western Passage proposed a submersible AI data center in the Bay of Fundy, tidal-turbine powered. Portugal: SIN01 (Sines) uses Atlantic seawater cooling.
- Gallup poll (March 2026): 70% of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their communities; more than half the world's population lives within 120 miles of a coast.
- Maintenance is a major challenge: a failed computer underwater cannot be repaired on site; the whole sealed module may need to be surfaced.
- **The main environmental concern involves the seawater used for cooling: discharging warm or hot water can potentially affect oxygen levels, pH and marine life in the surrounding waters.**
- **That heat is already apparent at the few seaborne data centers now operating. HiCloud, the engineering contractor for China's Hainan underwater data center, has reported a temperature increase of less than 1 degree Celsius (1.8 °F) in the seawater near the facility. SIN01 in Sines, Portugal, also returns seawater about 1 °C warmer.**
- Many marine species depend on stable water temperatures for breeding, feeding and migration; heat released by multiple underwater data centers could create localized thermal pollution and alter marine ecosystems. UNESCO estimates about 60% of marine ecosystems are already degraded or used unsustainably.
- The ocean is already warming with the atmosphere; that warming is already threatening coral reef and mangrove ecosystems, seagrasses and other aspects of the marine food web. As warming continues, ocean waters will be less useful for cooling electronic equipment in some regions.

## Assessment
- `authoritative: yes` — Fortune is a top-tier outlet; the piece is a republished The Conversation expert article.
- Directly supports the "no large temperature increase" finding: HiCloud's Hainan facility reported <1 °C increase in nearby seawater (operator-reported, not an independent study). Does NOT report any ecosystem "distortion" / fisher-displacement finding; the ecosystem concern is framed as a general risk of warm-water discharge (oxygen levels, pH, marine life), consistent with the deoxygenation concern.
